United Kingdom
AR TICLE HISTOR Y
Compiled October 25, 2026
ABSTRACT
Three recurrent problems have emerged on short-claim fake-news detection: am-
biguous label mappings, unfair comparison with the long-article settings, and
ill-defined contributions of affective features. We tackle these three issues using
Multi-Transformer Sentimental LIAR: a controlled paradigm in which we compare
RoBERTa, ELECTRA, BERT and DistilBERT on official LIAR partitions under
one publicly revealed clear-label scheme. Text-only, sentiment, emotion, and joint
affectiveness setting were measured and compared for its accuracy, precision, recall,
F1 score, AUC of receiver operating characteristic curve, Matthew’s correlation
coefficient, model size, training time respectively. With joint affective input ELEC-
TRA has reached an accuracy of72.03%, an F1 score of 0.7626, and a Matthews
correlation coefficient of 0.4247.However, with solely text input, ELECTRA reached
82.03%accuracy, 0.8356 for F1 score and 0.6404 for Matthews correlation coefficient.
It proves that affectives augmentation is context-aware depending on encoder’s ar-
chitecture and sometimes can negatively affect its performance. DistilBERT obtains
70.76% accuracy with 66.96 Million parameters, a suitable deployment model. A
traceable claim screening is made possible via the reported method, well documented
algorithm, Gradio UI, the result is kept as support for human judgment.
KEYWORDS
fake news detection; LIAR dataset; Sentimental LIAR; multi-transformer;
ELECTRA; DistilBERT; sentiment and emotion ablation; Gradio deployment
1. Introduction
False and misleading claims burden journalism, platform moderation, public communi-
cation, and political decision-making because harmful content can circulate faster than
complete fact-checking reports ( 1–3, 25). Short claims are particularly difficult because
they provide little context, contain weak discourse structure, and may use ambiguous or
emotionally persuasive language ( 4–6). An automated classifier cannot establish factual
truth by itself, but it can support early screening by ranking suspicious claims for human
review.
CONTACT Touseef Tahir. Email: Touseef.Tahir@roehampton.ac.uk

Earlier studies demonstrate how strongly task definition affects performance. The
original LIAR benchmark reported 27.4% accuracy, subsequent speaker-profile and meta-
data extensions reported 41.5% and 45.7%, Sentimental LIAR reported approximately
70%, and a hard binary LIAR benchmark reported approximately 62% ( 4–6). Word
Embedding over Linguistic Features for Fake News Detection reported 96.73% accuracy
for long news articles (7); however, a complete article contains much more evidence than
an isolated claim, so this result is not directly comparable with LIAR.
These studies leave three research gaps. First, inconsistent binary-label mappings make
results difficult to compare. Second, short-claim and long-article results are sometimes
presented together even though they measure different prediction problems. Third,
affective features are often added without a matched text-only ablation across several
transformer encoders, so their actual contribution remains uncertain.
We address these gaps through one clear-label LIAR protocol, four matched trans-
former encoders, and controlled text-only, sentiment-augmented, emotion-augmented,
and joint affective experiments. The application supports newsroom triage, educational
fact-checking exercises, moderation research, and model comparison. ELECTRA reaches
72.03% accuracy with joint affective information and 82.03% with text alone. DistilBERT
provides the preferred deployment balance at 70.76% accuracy with fewer parameters.
Hypotheses..We test three hypotheses. First, matched encoders will produce different
error profiles because their pre-training objectives differ. Second, sentiment and emotion
features will not improve every encoder because they can duplicate contextual information
or introduce noisy tokens. Third, DistilBERT will retain sufficient predictive performance
for interactive deployment while using fewer parameters than the larger encoders.
Illustrative claim types..The task receives short statements rather than complete
articles. A clearly false example is “The United States Constitution requires the president
to be born in Washington, D.C. ” A clearly real example is “A United States presidential
term lasts four years. ” A context-dependent statement such as “Unemployment is at its
lowest level ever” requires a date, population, and comparison period. Such ambiguity
motivates careful label definition and human review.
The next section reviews the relevant literature and identifies the precise gap addressed
by the framework.
2. Literature Review
Fake-news detection is commonly understood as an inference problem built from three
broad evidence families: the linguistic content of an item, the social context in which
it is produced and propagated, and external knowledge used to verify its claims ( 1–
3). Content-based methods examine lexical choice, syntax, semantics, writing style,
and rhetorical framing, whereas context-based methods use information such as source
credibility, user engagement, and diffusion structure (1, 2). Knowledge-based approaches
instead compare a statement with trusted evidence or structured facts ( 2, 3). Evidence-
grounded benchmarks such as FEVER make this distinction explicit by pairing supported
or refuted decisions with textual evidence, rather than inferring veracity from claim
wording alone (21). These families are complementary, but they are not interchangeable.
Because LIAR consists of short political statements rather than complete articles or
propagation graphs, the present study focuses on content-derived evidence and treats its
2

predictions as screening signals rather than completed fact verification (4,21).
2.1. Short-claim fake news and the LIAR benchmark
Wang introduced LIAR as a short political-claim dataset with six truthfulness grades
and speaker metadata. The original hybrid convolutional neural network achieved 27.4%
accuracy, illustrating the difficulty of six-class claim classification ( 4). Later speaker-
profile and metadata methods reported 41.5% and 45.7% accuracy, while a hard binary
benchmark reported approximately 62% ( 5, 6). These improvements are important, but
differences in label conversion and feature availability prevent direct ranking. This study
addresses that limitation by disclosing one binary mapping and evaluating every model
on the same filtered partitions.
2.2. Affective augmentation theory
Sentiment and emotion describe rhetorical tone, but they do not provide external evidence
that a proposition is true or false (12, 13). Prior linguistic analysis has identified stylistic
and affective differences across unreliable news and political fact-checking categories,
while FakeFlow models changes in affective information across a document ( 26, 30).
Sentimental LIAR combined Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers
with affective and speaker-credit features and reported approximately 70% accuracy ( 5).
These results motivate affect-aware modeling, but they do not establish that sentiment
and emotion improve every transformer architecture. The unresolved gap is feature
necessity: affective information must be compared with a text-only baseline under
identical data and evaluation conditions. This study fills that gap through four controlled
feature settings for every encoder.
2.3. Explainability and multi-transformer ensembles
The four selected transformer encoders use different learning strategies: bidirectional
masked-token learning, optimized pre-training, replaced-token discrimination, and knowl-
edge distillation (8–11). Previous single-model studies cannot show whether a reported
gain arises from the feature design or the selected encoder. This study therefore uses a
matched four-model comparison and reports accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, area
under the receiver operating characteristic curve, and Matthews correlation coefficient
rather than relying on accuracy alone.
2.4. Deployment and responsible use
Interactive ML demos (Gradio) provide standardized claim-entry forms with metadata for
model choice and affective diagnostics ( 17). Those interfaces answer a different scientific
question,can a non-expert run the model?, from the notebook question,what Acc did
seed 42 yield?Transparent release should additionally state intended use, evaluation
conditions, and limitations, following the model-card principle for documented ML
deployment (23). Multi-Transformer Sentimental LIAR therefore uses Gradio only as
deployment context: compulsory claim text, optional affective display, and DistilBERT
as the efficiency default.
3

2.5. Research gap
Prior work leaves three linked limitations: inconsistent binary-label protocols, invalid
comparison between short claims and long articles, and insufficient matched ablation
of affective features across transformer architectures. We address these gaps with one
disclosed LIAR label mapping, strict separation of article and claim results, and four
controlled feature settings for each encoder.
The methodology section converts these gaps into a formal task, a controlled feature
design, and a matched multi-model architecture.
3. Methodology
The central problem addressed by this work is the absence of a scientifically honest
short-claim decision-support stack that can:
(1) Accept routine claim text required for fact-check screening;
(2) Produce false or real screening scores from matched transformers without mixing
long-article accuracy with short-claim accuracy; and
(3) Determine whether sentiment and emotion descriptors improve performance beyond
claim text alone.
Formally, letDL ={(xi,y i)}NL
i=1 be labeled LIAR claims with yi ∈ {0, 1}under
protocol hard clear, and let S be the set of affective settings. The learning objective
is to estimate p(y=1|˜xs) for each backbone m and setting s∈Swithout using any
WELFake article row. Existing approaches solve only subsets of this problem ( 5, 6, 8).
3.1. Framework design
Framework design explains how the scientific components operate as one controlled
system. It connects the prediction task, label definition, feature construction, transformer
encoders, ablation conditions, evaluation rules, and deployment criterion. The design
keeps the source data and target labels fixed while changing only the feature setting
and encoder. This isolation is essential because an observed performance difference
can otherwise result from a changed dataset, a different label mapping, or a different
test partition rather than from the model itself. The framework therefore supports two
comparisons: an architectural comparison among four encoders and a feature comparison
among four input settings. Both comparisons use the same official partitions and the
same binary task.
The framework also separates predictive modeling from factual verification. It learns
statistical associations from short claim text and optional affective descriptors, but
it does not retrieve supporting documents or validate a proposition against external
evidence. Evidence-aware systems such as DeClarE address a broader verification setting
by combining claims with retrieved evidence ( 28). In contrast, the present framework
is designed for early screening, controlled experimentation, and transparent model
comparison. This boundary determines how the results and the Gradio output should
be interpreted.

3.1.4. Model selection rationale
The four encoders were selected because they represent complementary solutions to
limitations observed in earlier text classifiers. Classical bag-of-words and shallow neural
models have difficulty representing context, word order, negation, and long-range rela-
tions within a claim. Transformer self-attention supplies the shared contextual foundation
for the selected encoders ( 14). Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers
addresses this problem through bidirectional contextual pre-training, but its masked-
language objective and computational cost do not guarantee the best short-claim decision
boundary (8). Robustly Optimized Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Trans-
formers improves the pre-training recipe and can strengthen contextual representations,
although its larger parameter count increases resource demand ( 9). Efficiently Learn-
ing an Encoder that Classifies Token Replacements Accurately uses replaced-token
discrimination, which provides a learning signal at more token positions and may be
advantageous when claims are short ( 11). Distilled Bidirectional Encoder Represen-
tations from Transformers transfers knowledge from a larger teacher into a smaller
model, making it suitable for interactive deployment, although compression can reduce
predictive capacity (10). Evaluating all four models under matched conditions reveals
whether performance differences arise from architecture rather than from inconsistent
datasets or label rules.

3.2. Dataset and task design

3.2.2. Dataset and labels

The methodology defines the data, target labels, features, and model family. The
experimental setup now specifies how these components are trained and evaluated.
4. Experimental Setup
The experimental setup converts the methodology into a reproducible evaluation proce-
dure. The methodology defines the data, labels, features, and model family; this section
defines how the models are trained, how decisions are selected, and how performance
is measured. All four encoders use the same retained claims and official partitions.
The comparison therefore changes the encoder or feature setting without changing the
underlying test population. This separation reduces confounding and ensures that later
differences can be interpreted as model or feature effects rather than as consequences of
inconsistent data preparation.
The setup follows a strict training, validation, and testing sequence. Training data
estimate model parameters. Validation data control early stopping and decision-threshold
selection. Test data remain isolated until the final evaluation. The reported run uses
seed 42 so that its outputs can be reproduced, but a single seed cannot estimate
optimization variance. Repeated runs and complete configuration reporting remain
necessary for stronger reproducibility claims (24,32).
4.1. Training protocol
All encoders use the same filtered LIAR partitions and a common transformer fine-tuning
workflow (15). Training uses class-weighted loss, early stopping, and threshold selection
on the validation partition. The test partition remains untouched until final evaluation.
Seed 42 fixes the reported run. Because only one seed was executed, the experiment
8

establishes reproducibility for that run but does not estimate variation across random
initializations (24).
4.2. Evaluation measures
We report accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, area under the receiver operating char-
acteristic curve, and Matthews correlation coefficient ( 16, 18, 19). Receiver operating
characteristic curves and precision and recall curves describe threshold behavior. Param-
eter counts and training time describe computational cost. Controlled ablation compares
text-only, sentiment-augmented, emotion-augmented, and joint affective inputs.
4.3. Statistical comparison
Pairwise model comparison should use McNemar’s test on the same test claims ( 35).
Let n01 denote claims classified correctly by model one and incorrectly by model two,
and letn 10 denote the reverse disagreements. The continuity-corrected statistic is
χ2 = (|n01−n10|−1)2

The available experiment summary preserves aggregate metrics and confusion matrices
but not the paired claim-level prediction vectors required to calculate n01 and n10. We
therefore do not report a fabricated significance value. A future evaluation export must
retain claim identifiers, labels, and predictions for every model so that McNemar p-values
and confidence intervals can be computed.
4.4. Probability calibration
The models produce scores for ranking and thresholding. These scores are not automati-
cally calibrated probabilities of truth. Calibration should be measured on held-out data
with reliability diagrams, expected calibration error, the Brier score, and calibration-
sensitive comparison of learning algorithms before an interface displays probability
language ( 22, 36, 37). The current application presents model scores as screening
outputs and avoids interpreting them as verified confidence.
This setup separates model design from evaluation decisions. The next section reports
the locked numerical results without changing the protocol after observing the test set.
5. Results
This section reports the complete evidence for the four transformer encoders. It first
presents the joint affective comparison, then examines text-only, sentiment-augmented,
emotion-augmented, and joint affective ablations. Receiver operating characteristic
and precision and recall curves describe threshold behavior, while parameter counts
and training times support the deployment decision. Under the joint affective setting,
ELECTRA achieves72.03%accuracy, an F1 score of 0.7626, an area under the receiver
operating characteristic curve of 0.7909, and a Matthews correlation coefficient of
0.4247. The strongest overall result is ELECTRA with text alone at82.03%accuracy.

5.2. Four-model hold-out comparison
The hold-out comparison examines generalization on the untouched test partition after

claims, their errors are comparable at the instance level even though paired prediction

that a small score difference will persist across seeds or domains.

5.3. Ablation and error analysis
The ablation analysis tests whether sentiment and emotion add useful information beyond
the claim text already encoded by each transformer. It changes one feature condition at
a time while preserving the label protocol and data partitions. This controlled design
distinguishes a genuine feature contribution from a gain caused by a different dataset or
test sample. Tables 6 to 8 report exact accuracy, F1 score, and Matthews correlation
coefficient values for text-only, sentiment-augmented, emotion-augmented, and joint
affective inputs. Figure 4 retains the grouped visual comparison so that architecture-
specific patterns remain visible.
The three measures answer different questions. Accuracy measures total correctness
but can conceal class preference. The F1 score emphasizes the precision and recall
balance for the positive class but excludes true negatives. The Matthews correlation
coefficient incorporates the complete confusion matrix and exposes degenerate behavior.
This distinction is essential for the ELECTRA emotion-only condition: its accuracy
appears non-trivial, but its zero Matthews correlation coefficient indicates that the
predictions contain no useful balanced association with the observed labels.

5.5. Qualitative error analysis
Short claims fail for identifiable linguistic reasons. Numerical claims often omit a date,
denominator, or comparison group. Negation can reverse a claim while preserving most of
its vocabulary. Entity substitutions can make a linguistically plausible sentence factually
wrong. Quoted speech can also cause the model to attribute a statement to the wrong
speaker. Affective tags do not resolve these problems because none supplies external
evidence.
Representative misclassification patterns.Table 9 records concrete examples for
qualitative audit. The aggregate result package does not retain the claim-level text
and paired predictions needed to assert that these exact sentences were test-set errors.
The table therefore presents representative error patterns rather than fabricated test
instances.
5.6. Why text-only ELECTRA performs best
Results show that ELECTRA performs best without appended affective tags. Three
mechanisms explain this outcome. First, replaced-token discrimination already trains
ELECTRA to detect locally inconsistent wording, which is valuable for short claims (11).
Second, sentiment and emotion descriptors repeat information that the contextual encoder
can infer from the original text. This redundancy consumes sequence capacity without
adding factual evidence. Third, serialized tags alter token positions and attention patterns.
Noisy or weakly relevant emotion tokens can therefore shift the decision boundary away
from the claim itself. The decline from 82.03% text-only accuracy to 72.03% joint affective
accuracy supports this explanation. The result does not show that affect is always useless.
It shows that feature value depends on the encoder, task, and serialization method.

5.7. Literature and capability comparison
Tables 10 to 11 compare the framework with representative short-claim, affect-aware,
transformer, and long-article systems ( 5–7). The comparison serves two purposes. First,
it places the reported accuracy values within their correct task definitions. A six-class
LIAR result, a binary LIAR result, and a long-article result use different target spaces and
evidence conditions. Their numerical values cannot support a direct universal ranking.
Second, the comparison examines methodological coverage. It asks whether each system
discloses its label protocol, evaluates several encoders under matched conditions, tests
affective features through ablation, reports balanced measures such as the Matthews
correlation coefficient and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve,
and provides an accessible application.
Table 10 therefore emphasizes construct validity rather than numerical competition.
Sentimental LIAR provides the closest affect-aware comparison, but it uses a different
label conversion. The Khan benchmark provides a difficult binary reference, while
WELFake demonstrates the higher performance achievable when complete articles
supply more linguistic evidence. The transformer rows show that using a strong encoder
alone does not guarantee a fair comparison. Dataset control, label disclosure, feature
control, and consistent evaluation remain necessary.
Table 11 extends the analysis beyond accuracy. The proposed framework combines
four elements that earlier pipelines usually address separately: matched transformer
evaluation, explicit affective ablation, multi-measure reporting, and Gradio deployment.
This combination supports an integration contribution. It does not claim that the
individual encoders, sentiment lexicon, emotion lexicon, or interface technology are
independently novel.

one selected operating point. This analysis matters because accuracy, precision, recall,
F1 score, and Matthews correlation coefficient depend on a particular threshold. Two
models can produce similar threshold-specific scores while ranking claims differently
across the full score range.

6. Discussion
6.1. Scientific interpretation
Matched multi-transformer evaluation reveals errors that a single-model accuracy score
would hide (5, 6). ELECTRA achieves 72.03% accuracy with joint affective information
and 82.03% with text alone. Sentimental LIAR reports approximately 70% under a
different label mapping, while the higher WELFake result concerns long articles ( 5, 7).
Keeping these tasks separate prevents an invalid comparison.
6.2. Theoretical implications of affective augmentation
Affective features can help when lexical sentiment captures rhetorical framing that the
encoder underrepresents. They can hurt when the tags duplicate contextual information,
exaggerate emotionally charged but truthful language, or introduce tokens unrelated to
factuality (5, 12, 13). The results support the second hypothesis: feature value depends
on the encoder. RoBERTa gains slightly in selected emotion-based conditions, whereas
ELECTRA and BERT perform best with text alone. The evidence therefore rejects a
universal claim that sentiment and emotion improve fake-news detection.
6.3. Operational implications
Model choice depends on the screening objective. ELECTRA provides the strongest over-
all discrimination. RoBERTa provides the highest recall and suits settings where missed
target claims carry the greatest cost. DistilBERT provides the strongest resource profile
for interactive use. These roles should remain separate because analytical leadership,
recall-oriented screening, and deployment efficiency optimize different objectives.
6.4. Interpretation of the hypotheses
The results support the first hypothesis because the encoders produce different metric
and error profiles under matched conditions. They support the second hypothesis because
affective augmentation helps some configurations but reduces ELECTRA performance.
The deployment evidence supports the third hypothesis because DistilBERT retains

feature design, and operational use without treating one metric as sufficient.
The discussion establishes what the results mean. The next section translates the
efficiency decision into an interactive screening workflow.
7. Deployment
Deployment translates the evaluated pipeline into an accessible inference workflow
without changing the training data, evaluation protocol, or reported test results. Gradio
exposes the selected DistilBERT model and affective diagnostics, while model-card-style
documentation states the intended use, operating conditions, and limitations ( 17, 23).
The classifier neither retrieves evidence nor produces calibrated truth probabilities. Its
output supports screening and prioritization rather than final fact-checking (21,22).
7.1. Model packaging
The trained model is packaged with its label protocol, feature setting, intended screening
use, evaluation measures, and limitations. This documentation follows the core model-
card principle of making operating conditions explicit (23).
7.2. Gradio interface
The Gradio application requires claim text and returns a model label, a screening score,
and affective diagnostics ( 17). Figure 8 shows the interface layout used to organize
claim entry, DistilBERT inference, screening output, affective diagnostics, and the
responsible-use warning.
19

7.3. End-to-end deployment process
The deployment process follows the experimental sequence. The system filters LIAR
claims with the clear-label rule, computes affective descriptors, applies the selected
transformer, and displays the result for human review. Model selection considers predic-
tive performance and computational cost together. The interface does not convert the
classifier into an evidence-retrieval or truth-verification system.
8. Limitations and Future Work
This section defines the boundary of the reported evidence and converts each limitation
into a concrete research direction. The results establish performance for one clear-label
conversion of English political claims, one fixed random seed, and one in-domain test
partition. They do not establish stability across repeated fine-tuning runs, calibrated
probabilities, fairness across demographic or political subgroups, or generalization to
other topics and languages. The deployed interface also remains a screening tool because
the model does not retrieve evidence or verify claims against primary sources. Stating
these limits prevents the strong in-domain results from being interpreted as universal
fact-checking performance.
8.1. Single-seed and statistical uncertainty
The reported experiment uses one fixed seed. This design makes the run reproducible
but does not quantify variation across random initializations ( 24, 32). Future work
should repeat every model and feature setting across several seeds and report the mean,
standard deviation, confidence interval, and rank stability. The next evaluation should
also retain paired claim-level predictions so that McNemar tests can compare models
without reconstructing invalid statistics from aggregate confusion matrices (35).
8.2. Calibration and subgroup evaluation
The study does not evaluate probability calibration or subgroup performance. Interface
scores must therefore not be interpreted as calibrated probabilities of truth ( 22, 23).
Future experiments should report reliability diagrams, expected calibration error, Brier
score, and calibration before and after temperature scaling ( 36, 37). They should also
report performance across speakers, topics, parties, and time periods when ethically
and statistically appropriate. Dataset and model documentation should record these
evaluations so that deployment conditions remain visible (23,34).
8.3. Cross-domain generalizability
LIAR contains English political claims from one fact-checking context. Performance can
change for health misinformation, disaster rumors, financial claims, other countries, other
languages, or complete news articles. The present results therefore establish in-domain
short-claim performance only. Future work should test external claim datasets such as
MultiFC, conduct temporal validation, and evaluate domain adaptation before deploy-
ment outside the LIAR setting ( 27, 29, 31). It should also measure performance under
explicit distribution shifts because pretrained transformers can lose accuracy outside the
20

training distribution, and compression does not guarantee equal robustness (38). A struc-
tured benchmark design similar to WILDS would help separate temporal, geographic,
topical, and source shifts instead of reporting one combined external score (39).
8.4. Evidence and application limits
The system does not retrieve primary sources, model multimodal evidence, or verify
numerical claims against external databases. Affective tag serialization also provides a
simple auxiliary representation rather than learned multimodal fusion. Future work should
combine claim classification with evidence retrieval and ranking, following evidence-aware
and benchmark-based fact-checking research ( 21, 28, 29). It should then evaluate how
journalists and researchers use the output rather than assuming that interface availability
proves practical benefit (33). Until then, outputs should support human review rather
than replace it (1,2).
8.5. Future research roadmap
Future work should proceed in five stages. First, repeated multi-seed experiments
should quantify optimization uncertainty and test whether encoder rankings remain
stable (24, 32). Second, claim-level prediction records should support McNemar tests,
bootstrap confidence intervals, and transparent error comparisons (35). Third, calibration
experiments should compare raw scores, temperature scaling, reliability diagrams, and
Brier scores before the interface uses probability language ( 22, 36, 37). Fourth, external
evaluation should cover MultiFC, temporal splits, multilingual claims, and controlled
distribution shifts ( 27, 38, 39). Fifth, behavioral test suites should perturb names,
quantities, negation, dates, and emotional wording to reveal model invariances and
brittle shortcuts that aggregate accuracy cannot expose (40).
The longer-term system should integrate retrieval, evidence ranking, verdict predic-
tion, and explanation while preserving the present distinction between screening and
verification (21, 28, 29). Human-centered trials should measure review time, false-
alarm burden, trust calibration, and correction quality for journalists, educators, and
moderation researchers (33). These extensions would transform the current controlled
classifier into a more complete and responsibly evaluated fact-checking assistant without
overstating what claim text alone can establish.
These limitations define the boundary of the contribution and motivate the final
conclusion.
9. Conclusion
Multi-Transformer Sentimental LIAR integrates clear-label LIAR claims, sentiment and
emotion descriptors, four matched transformer encoders, systematic ablation, and a
Gradio application without mixing article and claim accuracy. ELECTRA achieves
72.03% accuracy under the joint affective setting and 82.03% with text alone, demon-
strating that affective augmentation is architecture-dependent. DistilBERT remains
suitable for deployment at 70.76% accuracy with 66.96 million parameters. The study
therefore provides a well-defined path from short-claim data to comparative evaluation
and efficient interactive screening.

clean: ARTICLE TEMPLATE A Multi-Transformer Framework for Short-Claim Fake News Detection with Affective Feature Ablation Ali Saeeda, Nauman Irshad Ali Shah b, Touseef Tahirc,*, Danyal Tanveerb, Abdullah Ahmedb and Muhammad Shahroz Butt b aDepartment of Software Engineering, Faculty of IT & CS, University of Central Punjab, Lahore, Pakistan; bDepartment of Computer Science, University of Central Punjab, Lahore, 54000, Pakistan; cSchool of Computing, Engineering and the Built Environment, London, United Kingdom AR TICLE HISTOR Y Compiled October 25, 2026 ABSTRACT Three recurrent problems have emerged on short-claim fake-news detection: ambiguous label mappings, unfair comparison with the long-article settings, and ill-defined contributions of affective features. We tackle these three issues using Multi-Transformer Sentimental LIAR: a controlled paradigm in which we compare RoBERTa, ELECTRA, BERT and DistilBERT on official LIAR partitions under one publicly revealed clear-label scheme. Text-only, sentiment, emotion, and joint affectiveness setting were measured and compared for its accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, AUC of receiver operating characteristic curve, Matthew’s correlation coefficient, model size, training time respectively. With joint affective input ELECTRA has reached an accuracy of72.03%, an F1 score of 0.7626, and a Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.4247.However, with solely text input, ELECTRA reached 82.03%accuracy, 0.8356 for F1 score and 0.6404 for Matthews correlation coefficient. It proves that affectives augmentation is context-aware depending on encoder’s architecture and sometimes can negatively affect its performance. DistilBERT obtains 70.76% accuracy with 66.96 Million parameters, a suitable deployment model. A traceable claim screening is made possible via the reported method, well documented algorithm, Gradio UI, the result is kept as support for human judgment. KEYWORDS fake news detection; LIAR dataset; Sentimental LIAR; multi-transformer; ELECTRA; DistilBERT; sentiment and emotion ablation; Gradio deployment 1. Introduction False and misleading claims burden journalism, platform moderation, public communication, and political decision-making because harmful content can circulate faster than complete fact-checking reports ( 1–3, 25). Short claims are particularly difficult because they provide little context, contain weak discourse structure, and may use ambiguous or emotionally persuasive language ( 4–6). An automated classifier cannot establish factual truth by itself, but it can support early screening by ranking suspicious claims for human review. CONTACT Touseef Tahir. Email: Touseef.Tahir@roehampton.ac.uk

Earlier studies demonstrate how strongly task definition affects performance. The original LIAR benchmark reported 27.4% accuracy, subsequent speaker-profile and metadata extensions reported 41.5% and 45.7%, Sentimental LIAR reported approximately 70%, and a hard binary LIAR benchmark reported approximately 62% ( 4–6). Word Embedding over Linguistic Features for Fake News Detection reported 96.73% accuracy for long news articles (7); however, a complete article contains much more evidence than an isolated claim, so this result is not directly comparable with LIAR. These studies leave three research gaps. First, inconsistent binary-label mappings make results difficult to compare. Second, short-claim and long-article results are sometimes presented together even though they measure different prediction problems. Third, affective features are often added without a matched text-only ablation across several transformer encoders, so their actual contribution remains uncertain. We address these gaps through one clear-label LIAR protocol, four matched transformer encoders, and controlled text-only, sentiment-augmented, emotion-augmented, and joint affective experiments. The application supports newsroom triage, educational fact-checking exercises, moderation research, and model comparison. ELECTRA reaches 72.03% accuracy with joint affective information and 82.03% with text alone. DistilBERT provides the preferred deployment balance at 70.76% accuracy with fewer parameters. Hypotheses..We test three hypotheses. First, matched encoders will produce different error profiles because their pre-training objectives differ. Second, sentiment and emotion features will not improve every encoder because they can duplicate contextual information or introduce noisy tokens. Third, DistilBERT will retain sufficient predictive performance for interactive deployment while using fewer parameters than the larger encoders. Illustrative claim types..The task receives short statements rather than complete articles. A clearly false example is “The United States Constitution requires the president to be born in Washington, D.C. ” A clearly real example is “A United States presidential term lasts four years. ” A context-dependent statement such as “Unemployment is at its lowest level ever” requires a date, population, and comparison period. Such ambiguity motivates careful label definition and human review. The next section reviews the relevant literature and identifies the precise gap addressed by the framework. 2. Literature Review Fake-news detection is commonly understood as an inference problem built from three broad evidence families: the linguistic content of an item, the social context in which it is produced and propagated, and external knowledge used to verify its claims ( 1– 3). Content-based methods examine lexical choice, syntax, semantics, writing style, and rhetorical framing, whereas context-based methods use information such as source credibility, user engagement, and diffusion structure (1, 2). Knowledge-based approaches instead compare a statement with trusted evidence or structured facts ( 2, 3). Evidencegrounded benchmarks such as FEVER make this distinction explicit by pairing supported or refuted decisions with textual evidence, rather than inferring veracity from claim wording alone (21). These families are complementary, but they are not interchangeable. Because LIAR consists of short political statements rather than complete articles or propagation graphs, the present study focuses on content-derived evidence and treats its

predictions as screening signals rather than completed fact verification (4,21). 2.1. Short-claim fake news and the LIAR benchmark Wang introduced LIAR as a short political-claim dataset with six truthfulness grades and speaker metadata. The original hybrid convolutional neural network achieved 27.4% accuracy, illustrating the difficulty of six-class claim classification ( 4). Later speakerprofile and metadata methods reported 41.5% and 45.7% accuracy, while a hard binary benchmark reported approximately 62% ( 5, 6). These improvements are important, but differences in label conversion and feature availability prevent direct ranking. This study addresses that limitation by disclosing one binary mapping and evaluating every model on the same filtered partitions. 2.2. Affective augmentation theory Sentiment and emotion describe rhetorical tone, but they do not provide external evidence that a proposition is true or false (12, 13). Prior linguistic analysis has identified stylistic and affective differences across unreliable news and political fact-checking categories, while FakeFlow models changes in affective information across a document ( 26, 30). Sentimental LIAR combined Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers with affective and speaker-credit features and reported approximately 70% accuracy ( 5). These results motivate affect-aware modeling, but they do not establish that sentiment and emotion improve every transformer architecture. The unresolved gap is feature necessity: affective information must be compared with a text-only baseline under identical data and evaluation conditions. This study fills that gap through four controlled feature settings for every encoder. 2.3. Explainability and multi-transformer ensembles The four selected transformer encoders use different learning strategies: bidirectional masked-token learning, optimized pre-training, replaced-token discrimination, and knowledge distillation (8–11). Previous single-model studies cannot show whether a reported gain arises from the feature design or the selected encoder. This study therefore uses a matched four-model comparison and reports accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, and Matthews correlation coefficient rather than relying on accuracy alone. 2.4. Deployment and responsible use Interactive ML demos (Gradio) provide standardized claim-entry forms with metadata for model choice and affective diagnostics ( 17). Those interfaces answer a different scientific question,can a non-expert run the model?, from the notebook question,what Acc did seed 42 yield?Transparent release should additionally state intended use, evaluation conditions, and limitations, following the model-card principle for documented ML deployment (23). Multi-Transformer Sentimental LIAR therefore uses Gradio only as deployment context: compulsory claim text, optional affective display, and DistilBERT as the efficiency default.

2.5. Research gap Prior work leaves three linked limitations: inconsistent binary-label protocols, invalid comparison between short claims and long articles, and insufficient matched ablation of affective features across transformer architectures. We address these gaps with one disclosed LIAR label mapping, strict separation of article and claim results, and four controlled feature settings for each encoder. The methodology section converts these gaps into a formal task, a controlled feature design, and a matched multi-model architecture. 3. Methodology The central problem addressed by this work is the absence of a scientifically honest short-claim decision-support stack that can: (1) Accept routine claim text required for fact-check screening; (2) Produce false or real screening scores from matched transformers without mixing long-article accuracy with short-claim accuracy; and (3) Determine whether sentiment and emotion descriptors improve performance beyond claim text alone. Formally, letDL ={(xi,y i)}NL i=1 be labeled LIAR claims with yi ∈ {0, 1}under protocol hard clear, and let S be the set of affective settings. The learning objective is to estimate p(y=1| ̃xs) for each backbone m and setting s∈Swithout using any WELFake article row. Existing approaches solve only subsets of this problem ( 5, 6, 8). 3.1. Framework design Framework design explains how the scientific components operate as one controlled system. It connects the prediction task, label definition, feature construction, transformer encoders, ablation conditions, evaluation rules, and deployment criterion. The design keeps the source data and target labels fixed while changing only the feature setting and encoder. This isolation is essential because an observed performance difference can otherwise result from a changed dataset, a different label mapping, or a different test partition rather than from the model itself. The framework therefore supports two comparisons: an architectural comparison among four encoders and a feature comparison among four input settings. Both comparisons use the same official partitions and the same binary task. The framework also separates predictive modeling from factual verification. It learns statistical associations from short claim text and optional affective descriptors, but it does not retrieve supporting documents or validate a proposition against external evidence. Evidence-aware systems such as DeClarE address a broader verification setting by combining claims with retrieved evidence ( 28). In contrast, the present framework is designed for early screening, controlled experimentation, and transparent model comparison. This boundary determines how the results and the Gradio output should be interpreted. 3.1.1. Model selection rationale The four encoders were selected because they represent complementary solutions to limitations observed in earlier text classifiers. Classical bag-of-words and shallow neural models have difficulty representing context, word order, negation, and long-range relations within a claim. Transformer self-attention supplies the shared contextual foundation for the selected encoders ( 14). Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers addresses this problem through bidirectional contextual pre-training, but its maskedlanguage objective and computational cost do not guarantee the best short-claim decision boundary (8). Robustly Optimized Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers improves the pre-training recipe and can strengthen contextual representations, although its larger parameter count increases resource demand ( 9). Efficiently Learning an Encoder that Classifies Token Replacements Accurately uses replaced-token discrimination, which provides a learning signal at more token positions and may be advantageous when claims are short ( 11). Distilled Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers transfers knowledge from a larger teacher into a smaller model, making it suitable for interactive deployment, although compression can reduce predictive capacity (10). Evaluating all four models under matched conditions reveals whether performance differences arise from architecture rather than from inconsistent datasets or label rules.

The experimental setup now specifies how these components are trained and evaluated. 4. Experimental Setup The experimental setup converts the methodology into a reproducible evaluation procedure. The methodology defines the data, labels, features, and model family; this section defines how the models are trained, how decisions are selected, and how performance is measured. All four encoders use the same retained claims and official partitions. The comparison therefore changes the encoder or feature setting without changing the underlying test population. This separation reduces confounding and ensures that later differences can be interpreted as model or feature effects rather than as consequences of inconsistent data preparation. The setup follows a strict training, validation, and testing sequence. Training data estimate model parameters. Validation data control early stopping and decision-threshold selection. Test data remain isolated until the final evaluation. The reported run uses seed 42 so that its outputs can be reproduced, but a single seed cannot estimate optimization variance. Repeated runs and complete configuration reporting remain necessary for stronger reproducibility claims (24,32). 4.1. Training protocol All encoders use the same filtered LIAR partitions and a common transformer fine-tuning workflow (15). Training uses class-weighted loss, early stopping, and threshold selection on the validation partition. The test partition remains untouched until final evaluation. Seed 42 fixes the reported run. Because only one seed was executed, the experiment

establishes reproducibility for that run but does not estimate variation across random initializations (24). 4.2. Evaluation measures We report accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, and Matthews correlation coefficient ( 16, 18, 19). Receiver operating characteristic curves and precision and recall curves describe threshold behavior. Parameter counts and training time describe computational cost. Controlled ablation compares text-only, sentiment-augmented, emotion-augmented, and joint affective inputs. 4.3. Statistical comparison Pairwise model comparison should use McNemar’s test on the same test claims ( 35). Let n01 denote claims classified correctly by model one and incorrectly by model two, and letn 10 denote the reverse disagreements. The continuity-corrected statistic is χ2 = (|n01−n10|−1)2 n01 +n 10 .(4) The available experiment summary preserves aggregate metrics and confusion matrices but not the paired claim-level prediction vectors required to calculate n01 and n10. We therefore do not report a fabricated significance value. A future evaluation export must retain claim identifiers, labels, and predictions for every model so that McNemar p-values and confidence intervals can be computed. 4.4. Probability calibration The models produce scores for ranking and thresholding. These scores are not automatically calibrated probabilities of truth. Calibration should be measured on held-out data with reliability diagrams, expected calibration error, the Brier score, and calibrationsensitive comparison of learning algorithms before an interface displays probability language ( 22, 36, 37). The current application presents model scores as screening outputs and avoids interpreting them as verified confidence. This setup separates model design from evaluation decisions. The next section reports the locked numerical results without changing the protocol after observing the test set. 5. Qualitative error analysis Short claims fail for identifiable linguistic reasons. Numerical claims often omit a date, denominator, or comparison group. Negation can reverse a claim while preserving most of its vocabulary. Entity substitutions can make a linguistically plausible sentence factually wrong. Quoted speech can also cause the model to attribute a statement to the wrong speaker. Affective tags do not resolve these problems because none supplies external evidence. Why text-only ELECTRA performs best Results show that ELECTRA performs best without appended affective tags. Three mechanisms explain this outcome. First, replaced-token discrimination already trains ELECTRA to detect locally inconsistent wording, which is valuable for short claims (11). Second, sentiment and emotion descriptors repeat information that the contextual encoder can infer from the original text. This redundancy consumes sequence capacity without adding factual evidence. Third, serialized tags alter token positions and attention patterns. Noisy or weakly relevant emotion tokens can therefore shift the decision boundary away from the claim itself. The decline from 82.03% text-only accuracy to 72.03% joint affective accuracy supports this explanation. The result does not show that affect is always useless. It shows that feature value depends on the encoder, task, and serialization method.

Scientific interpretation Matched multi-transformer evaluation reveals errors that a single-model accuracy score would hide (5, 6). ELECTRA achieves 72.03% accuracy with joint affective information and 82.03% with text alone. Sentimental LIAR reports approximately 70% under a different label mapping, while the higher WELFake result concerns long articles ( 5, 7). Keeping these tasks separate prevents an invalid comparison. 6.2. Theoretical implications of affective augmentation Affective features can help when lexical sentiment captures rhetorical framing that the encoder underrepresents. They can hurt when the tags duplicate contextual information, exaggerate emotionally charged but truthful language, or introduce tokens unrelated to factuality (5, 12, 13). The results support the second hypothesis: feature value depends on the encoder. RoBERTa gains slightly in selected emotion-based conditions, whereas ELECTRA and BERT perform best with text alone. The evidence therefore rejects a universal claim that sentiment and emotion improve fake-news detection. 6.3. Operational implications Model choice depends on the screening objective. ELECTRA provides the strongest overall discrimination. RoBERTa provides the highest recall and suits settings where missed target claims carry the greatest cost. DistilBERT provides the strongest resource profile for interactive use. These roles should remain separate because analytical leadership, recall-oriented screening, and deployment efficiency optimize different objectives. 6.4. Interpretation of the hypotheses The results support the first hypothesis because the encoders produce different metric and error profiles under matched conditions. They support the second hypothesis because affective augmentation helps some configurations but reduces ELECTRA performance. These findings connect architecture, feature design, and operational use without treating one metric as sufficient. The discussion establishes what the results mean. The next section translates the efficiency decision into an interactive screening workflow. 7. Deployment Deployment translates the evaluated pipeline into an accessible inference workflow without changing the training data, evaluation protocol, or reported test results. Gradio exposes the selected DistilBERT model and affective diagnostics, while model-card-style documentation states the intended use, operating conditions, and limitations ( 17, 23). The classifier neither retrieves evidence nor produces calibrated truth probabilities. Its output supports screening and prioritization rather than final fact-checking (21,22). 7.1. Model packaging The trained model is packaged with its label protocol, feature setting, intended screening use, evaluation measures, and limitations. This documentation follows the core modelcard principle of making operating conditions explicit (23). 7.2. Gradio interface The Gradio application requires claim text and returns a model label, a screening score, and affective diagnostics ( 17). Figure 8 shows the interface layout used to organize claim entry, DistilBERT inference, screening output, affective diagnostics, and the responsible-use warning.

7.3. End-to-end deployment process The deployment process follows the experimental sequence. The system filters LIAR claims with the clear-label rule, computes affective descriptors, applies the selected transformer, and displays the result for human review. Model selection considers predictive performance and computational cost together. The interface does not convert the classifier into an evidence-retrieval or truth-verification system. 8. Limitations and Future Work This section defines the boundary of the reported evidence and converts each limitation into a concrete research direction. The results establish performance for one clear-label conversion of English political claims, one fixed random seed, and one in-domain test partition. They do not establish stability across repeated fine-tuning runs, calibrated probabilities, fairness across demographic or political subgroups, or generalization to other topics and languages. The deployed interface also remains a screening tool because the model does not retrieve evidence or verify claims against primary sources. Stating these limits prevents the strong in-domain results from being interpreted as universal fact-checking performance. 8.1. Single-seed and statistical uncertainty The reported experiment uses one fixed seed. This design makes the run reproducible but does not quantify variation across random initializations ( 24, 32). Future work should repeat every model and feature setting across several seeds and report the mean, standard deviation, confidence interval, and rank stability. The next evaluation should also retain paired claim-level predictions so that McNemar tests can compare models without reconstructing invalid statistics from aggregate confusion matrices (35). 8.2. Calibration and subgroup evaluation The study does not evaluate probability calibration or subgroup performance. Interface scores must therefore not be interpreted as calibrated probabilities of truth ( 22, 23). Future experiments should report reliability diagrams, expected calibration error, Brier score, and calibration before and after temperature scaling ( 36, 37). They should also report performance across speakers, topics, parties, and time periods when ethically and statistically appropriate. Dataset and model documentation should record these evaluations so that deployment conditions remain visible (23,34). 8.3. Cross-domain generalizability LIAR contains English political claims from one fact-checking context. Performance can change for health misinformation, disaster rumors, financial claims, other countries, other languages, or complete news articles. The present results therefore establish in-domain short-claim performance only. Future work should test external claim datasets such as MultiFC, conduct temporal validation, and evaluate domain adaptation before deployment outside the LIAR setting ( 27, 29, 31). It should also measure performance under explicit distribution shifts because pretrained transformers can lose accuracy outside the

training distribution, and compression does not guarantee equal robustness (38). A structured benchmark design similar to WILDS would help separate temporal, geographic, topical, and source shifts instead of reporting one combined external score (39). 8.4. Evidence and application limits The system does not retrieve primary sources, model multimodal evidence, or verify numerical claims against external databases. Affective tag serialization also provides a simple auxiliary representation rather than learned multimodal fusion. Future work should combine claim classification with evidence retrieval and ranking, following evidence-aware and benchmark-based fact-checking research ( 21, 28, 29). It should then evaluate how journalists and researchers use the output rather than assuming that interface availability proves practical benefit (33). Until then, outputs should support human review rather than replace it (1,2). 8.5. Future research roadmap Future work should proceed in five stages. First, repeated multi-seed experiments should quantify optimization uncertainty and test whether encoder rankings remain stable (24, 32). Second, claim-level prediction records should support McNemar tests, bootstrap confidence intervals, and transparent error comparisons (35). Third, calibration experiments should compare raw scores, temperature scaling, reliability diagrams, and Brier scores before the interface uses probability language ( 22, 36, 37). Fourth, external evaluation should cover MultiFC, temporal splits, multilingual claims, and controlled distribution shifts ( 27, 38, 39). Fifth, behavioral test suites should perturb names, quantities, negation, dates, and emotional wording to reveal model invariances and brittle shortcuts that aggregate accuracy cannot expose (40). The longer-term system should integrate retrieval, evidence ranking, verdict prediction, and explanation while preserving the present distinction between screening and verification (21, 28, 29). Human-centered trials should measure review time, falsealarm burden, trust calibration, and correction quality for journalists, educators, and moderation researchers (33). These extensions would transform the current controlled classifier into a more complete and responsibly evaluated fact-checking assistant without overstating what claim text alone can establish. These limitations define the boundary of the contribution and motivate the final conclusion. 9. Conclusion Multi-Transformer Sentimental LIAR integrates clear-label LIAR claims, sentiment and emotion descriptors, four matched transformer encoders, systematic ablation, and a Gradio application without mixing article and claim accuracy. ELECTRA achieves 72.03% accuracy under the joint affective setting and 82.03% with text alone, demonstrating that affective augmentation is architecture-dependent. DistilBERT remains suitable for deployment at 70.76% accuracy with 66.96 million parameters. The study therefore provides a well-defined path from short-claim data to comparative evaluation and efficient interactive screening.

FakeFlow: Fake News Detection by Modeling the
Flow of Affective Information
Bilal Ghanem1, Simone Paolo Ponzetto 2, Paolo Rosso 1, Francisco Rangel 3
1Universitat Polit`ecnica de Val`encia, Spain
2University of Mannheim, Germany
3Symanto Research, Germany
bigha@doctor.upv.es, simone@informatik.uni-mannheim.de,
prosso@dsic.upv.es, francisco.rangel@symanto.com
Abstract
Fake news articles often stir the readers’ atten-
tion by means of emotional appeals that arouse
their feelings. Unlike in short news texts, au-
thors of longer articles can exploit such affec-
tive factors to manipulate readers by adding ex-
aggerations or fabricating events, in order to
affect the readers’ emotions. To capture this,
we propose in this paper to model the ﬂow of
affective information in fake news articles us-
ing a neural architecture. The proposed model,
FakeFlow, learns this ﬂow by combining topic
and affective information extracted from text.
We evaluate the model’s performance with sev-
eral experiments on four real-world datasets.
The results show that FakeFlow achieves su-
perior results when compared against state-of-
the-art methods, thus conﬁrming the impor-
tance of capturing the ﬂow of the affective in-
formation in news articles.
1 Introduction
In today’s information landscape, fake news are
used to manipulate public opinion (Zhou and Za-
farani, 2018) by reshaping readers’ opinions re-
garding some issues. In order to achieve this goal,
authors of fake news’ narratives need to capture the
interest of the reader. Thus, they are putting efforts
to make their news articles look more objective and
realistic. This is usually done by adding misleading
terms or events that can have a negative or positive
impact on the readers’ emotions.
Short text false information, e.g., fake claims or
misleading headlines, might be less harmful than
news articles. They may have some eye-catching
terms that aim to manipulate the readers’ emotions
(Chakraborty et al., 2016). In many cases, the iden-
tiﬁcation of this kind of exaggeration in short state-
ments can unmask the fabrication. On the other
hand, in fake news articles the authors exploit the
length of the news to conceal their fabricated story.
This fact exposes the readers to be emotionally
manipulated while reading longer texts that have
several imprecise or fabricated plots. The ﬂow
of information has been investigated for different
tasks: Reagan et al. (2016) studied the emotional
arcs in stories in order to understand complex emo-
tional trajectories; Maharjan et al. (2018) model
the ﬂow of emotions over a book and quantify its
usefulness for predicting success in books; Kar
et al. (2018) explore the problem of creating tags
for movies from plot synopses using emotions.
Unlike previous works (Rashkin et al., 2017; Shu
et al., 2018; Castelo et al., 2019; Ghanem et al.,
2020) that discarded the chronological order of
events in news articles, in this work we propose a
model that takes into account the affective changes
in texts to detect fake news. We hypothesize that
fake news has a different distribution of affective
information across the text compared to real news,
e.g. more fear emotion in the ﬁrst part of the article
or more overall offensive terms, etc. Therefore,
modeling the ﬂow of such information may help
discriminating fake from real news. Our model
consists of two main sub-modules, topic-based and
affective information detection. We combine these
two sub-modules since a news article’s topic may
have a correlation with its affective information.
For example, a fake news article about Islam or
Black people is likely to provoke fear and express
negative sentiment while another fake news that is
in favor of a particular politician might try to evoke
more positive emotions and also express some ex-
aggerations.
The contributions of our work are as follows:
• We design a model that detects fake news arti-
cles by taking into account the ﬂow of affective
information1.
1Available at https://github.com/bilalghanem/fake ﬂow

680
• Extensive experiments on four standard datasets
demonstrate the effectiveness of our model over
state-of-the-art alternatives.
• We build a novel fake news dataset, called Multi-
SourceFake, that is collected from a large set of
websites and annotated on the basis of the joint
agreement of a set of news sources.
2 Related Work
Previous work on fake news detection is mainly
divided into two main lines, namely with a focus
on social media (Zubiaga et al., 2015; Aker et al.,
2017; Ghanem et al., 2019) or online news articles
(Tausczik and Pennebaker, 2010; Horne and Adali,
2017; Rashkin et al., 2017; Barr ´on-Cedeno et al.,
2019). In this work we focus on the latter one. Fact-
checking (Karadzhov et al., 2017; Zlatkova et al.,
2019; Shu et al., 2019a) is another closely related
research topic. However, fact-checking targets only
short texts (that is, claims) and focuses on using
external resources (e.g. Web, knowledge sources)
to verify the factuality of the news. The focus in
previous work on fake news detection is mainly on
proposing new feature sets. Horne and Adali (2017)
present a set of content-based features, including
readability (number of unique words, SMOG read-
ability measure, etc.), stylistic (frequency of part-
of-speech tags, number of stop words, etc.) and psy-
cholinguistic features (i.e., several categories from
the LIWC dictionary (Tausczik and Pennebaker,
2010)). When these features are fed into a Support
Vector Machine (SVM) classiﬁer and applied, for
instance, to the task of distinguishing satire from
real news, they obtain high accuracies. Using the
same features for the task of fake news detection,
however, results in somewhat lower scores. P´erez-
Rosas et al. (2018) propose a model (FakeNewsDe-
tector) that uses a feature set consisting of unigrams
and bigrams, psycholinguistic, readability, punctu-
ation and dependency-based syntactic features, and
they evaluate the performance of their model in a
cross-domain experiment. Rashkin et al. (2017)
use a model based on ngram features with a Max-
Entropy classiﬁer and apply it to a dataset with
different types of fake news articles (e.g., satire,
hoax, propaganda, etc.). Similar to the previous
work, the authors evaluate their system’s perfor-
mance on in-domain and out-of-domain test sets,
respectively. News, and in particular fake news, are
dynamic in nature and change constantly. In order
to approach the dynamic nature of news, Castelo
et al. (2019) propose a topic-agnostic model (Top-
icAgnostic) that is based on morphological (count
of part-of-speech tags), psycholinguistic (personal
concerns, affection, and perception categories from
the LIWC dictionary), readability (Gunning Fog
metric, etc.) and Web-Markup features to capture
patterns of the Web pages’ layout (frequency of ad-
vertisements, presence of an author name, etc.). All
of the morphological, psycholinguistic and read-
ability features in the TopicAgnostic model were
extracted from headlines and texts of the news ar-
ticles. The approach obtains a better performance
than FakeNewsDetector on three different datasets
using a SVM classiﬁer. FakeNewsTracker (Shu
et al., 2019b) is a deep neural network-based model
that consists of two branches: one encodes news
article texts and the other encodes social media en-
gagements (e.g., tweets and their replies). A similar
model called Emotionally Infused Network (EIN)
is proposed in Ghanem et al. (2020). EIN encodes
the text of the article and their affective content,
based on several dictionaries, and then combines
the two vector representations. The authors evalu-
ate their model on a multi-class false information
dataset and show the effectiveness of using emo-
tion features extracted from the text. Despite the
large variety of features and models that have been
explored in previous work, none of these works
considers the sequence of affective information in
text; instead, they feed the entire news articles as
one segment into their models. In contrast, the aim
of our work is to evaluate this source of informa-
tion, using a neural architecture.
3 The FakeFlow Model
Given an input document, the FakeFlow model
ﬁrst divides it intoN segments. Then it uses both
word embeddings and other affective features such
as emotions, hyperbolic words , etc. in a way to
catch the ﬂow of emotions in the document. The
model learns to pay attention to the ﬂow of affective
information throughout the document, in order to
detect whether it is fake or real.
Figure 1 shows the architecture of the FakeFlow
model. The neural architecture has two main mod-
ules: The ﬁrst module uses a Convolutional Neural
Network (CNN) to extract topic-based information
from articles (left branch). The second module
models the ﬂow of the affective information within
the articles via Bidirectional Gated Recurrent Units
(Bi-GRUs) (right branch).

681
Figure 1: The architecture of the FakeFlow model.
3.1 Topic-based Information
Given a segmentn∈N of words, the model ﬁrst
embeds words to vectors through an embedding ma-
trix. Then it uses a CNN that applies convolution
processes and max pooling to get an abstractive
representation of the input segment. This repre-
sentation highlights important words, in which the
topic information of the segment is summarized.
Then it applies a fully connected layer on the out-
put segments to get a smaller representation (vtopic)
for later concatenation with the representation of
affective information:
vtopic =f (Wacnnv +ba)
whereWa andba are the corresponding weight ma-
trix and bias terms, andf is an activation function
such as ReLU, tanh, etc.
Key to FakeFlow is its ability to capture the rele-
vance of the affective information with respect to
the topics. For this, we concatenate the topic sum-
marized vectorvtopic with the representation vector
vaﬀect, aimed at capturing the affective information
extracted from each segment (Section 3.2).
vconcat =vtopic⊕vaﬀect
To merge the different representations and capture
their joint interaction in each segment, the model
processes the produced concatenated vectorvconcat
with another fully connected layer:
vf c =f (Wcvconcat +bc)
In order to create an attention-focused representa-
tion of the segments to highlight important ones
and to provide the model with the ability to weight
segments differently according to the similarity
of neighboring segments, the model applies a
context-aware self-attention mechanism (Zheng
et al., 2018) on vf c. This is a crucial step, as the
importance of a segment at timestep t is related
to the other segments since they share the same
context in the news article. Moreover, applying the
attention layer can help us understand which fea-
tures are most relevant by showing to which words
the network attends to during learning. The output
of the attention layer is an attention matrixlt with
scores for each token at each timestep.
3.2 Affective Flow of Information
To model the affective information ﬂow in the news
articles, we choose the following lexical features,
under the assumption that they have a different
distribution across the articles’ segments. We use
a term frequency representation weighted by the
articles’ length to extract the following features
from each segmentn:
• Emotions: We use emotions as features to detect
their change among articles’ segments. For that
we use the NRC emotions lexicon (Mohammad
and Turney, 2010) that contains ∼14K words
labeled using the eight Plutchik’s emotions ( 8
Features).
• Sentiment: We extract the sentiment from the
text, positive and negative, again using the NRC
lexicon (Mohammad and Turney, 2010) (2 Fea-
tures).
• Morality: We consider cue words from the Moral
Foundations Dictionary2 (Graham et al., 2009)
where words are assigned to one (or more) of the
following categories: care, harm, fairness, un-
fairness (cheating), loyalty, betrayal, authority,
subversion, sanctity and degradation (10 Fea-
tures).
• Imageability: We use a list of words rated by
their degree of abstractness and imageability 3.
These words have been extracted from the MRC
psycholinguistic database (Wilson, 1988) and
then using a supervised learning algorithm, the

3https://github.com/ytsvetko/metaphor/tree/master/
resources/imageability

682
words have been annotated by the degrees of
abstractness and imageability. The list contains
4,295 and 1,156 words rated by their degree of
abstractness and imageability, respectively ( 2
Features).
• Hyperbolic: We use a list of ∼350 hyperbolic
words (Chakraborty et al., 2016), i.e., words with
high positive or negative sentiment (e.g., terri-
fying, breathtakingly, soul-stirring, etc.). The
authors extracted these eye-catching words from
clickbaits news headlines (1 Feature).
To model the ﬂow of the above features, we rep-
resent each segment of an article by a vectorvaﬀect
capturing all 23 features listed above. Then we
feed the document’s vectors to a Bi-GRU network
to summarize the contextual ﬂow of the features
from both directions4 to obtainvﬂow .
Given the segments’ ﬂow representation (vﬂow )
of an article and their relevance to the topics (lt),
FakeFlow applies a dot product operation and then
averages the output matrix across the segments to
get a compact representation vcompact, which is
then fed into a fully connected layer:
vﬁnal =f (Wdvcompact +bd)
Finally, to generate the overall factuality label of
an article, a softmax layer is applied to the output
of the fully connected layer.
4 Fake News Datasets
Despite the recent efforts for debunking online fake
news, there is a dearth of publicly available datasets.
Most of the available datasets are small in size (e.g.,
the Politifact5 dataset in (Shu et al., 2018) has∼700
available articles, the Celebrity dataset in (P ´erez-
Rosas et al., 2018) has∼500 articles, etc.), their
test parts have not been manually annotated, or
have been collected from a very small number of
news sources. Nonetheless, we evaluate FakeFlow
on three different available datasets to demonstrate
its performance. In addition, we create our own
dataset. Table 1 gives an overview of the datasets
that we used in our work.
MultiSourceFake: We rely on different resources
for creating the training and test portions of the
dataset, so as to provide a challenging benchmark.
4During prototyping, GRU produced better overall results
than LSTM.
5https://www.politifact.com/
For the training part, we use OpenSources.co
(OS), MediaBiasFactCheck.com(MBFC), and Poli-
tiFact6 news websites’ lists. OS list contains 560
domains, MBFC list has 548 domains, and the Poli-
tiFact list has 227 domains. These lists have been
annotated by professional journalists. The lists con-
tain domains of online news websites annotated
based on the content type (as in the OS news list:
satire, reliable, etc.; and in the PolitiFact news list:
imposter, parody, fake news, etc.) or from a factu-
ality perspective (as in the MBFC news list: low,
medium, and high factuality). From the OS list,
we select domains that are in one of the following
categories: fake, bias, reliable, hate, satire, or con-
spiracy. We consider domains under the reliable
category as real news sources, and the rest as fake.
The PolitiFact list is different from the OS list since
it has only labels for domains that are either fake
or with mixed content. We discard the mixed ones7
and map the remaining ones to the fake news la-
bel. Finally, we select from the MBFC list those
domains that are annotated either as high or low
factual news and we map them to real and fake
labels, respectively. Out of these three ﬁnal lists,
we select only those domains for our dataset that
are annotated in all lists in a consistent way; for ex-
ample, we discard those domains that are annotated
as real in the OS list but their label in the MBFC
list is fake (low factuality). The ﬁnal list contains
85 news websites. We now proceed by projecting
the domain-level ground truth onto the content of
those domains and randomly sample articles, with
a maximum of 100 news articles per domain.8
For the test part, we use the leadstories.com fact
checking website for which professional journalists
annotated online news articles on the article level as
fake or real. We do not follow the way we annotate
the training part since the projection of the domain-
level ground truth inevitably introduces noise. The
journalists that annotated leadstories.com assigned
a set of labels to the fake news articles like, e.g.,
false, no evidence, satire, misleading, etc.; we map
them all to the fake label. In addition, we discard
all articles that are multimedia-based. After col-
lecting the news articles, we postprocess them by
discarding very short articles (less than 30 words).
The test part includes 689 fake news articles. We
complement the set with a sample of 1,000 real

using claims from PolitiFact and the other from
the GossipCop fact checking website. Given the
large number of true and false claims from these
two fact checking websites, Shu et al. (2018) built
news datasets that contain visual and textual news
articles content and social media information by
searching Twitter for users who shared news. Out
of the whole collected information, we use only the
textual information of news articles, which is the
part we are interested in.
5 Experiments
Experimental setup. We split the articles’ text
intoN segments and set the maximum length of
segments to 800 words, applying zero padding to
the ones shorter than 800 words. Concerning the
FakeFlow hyper-parameters, we tune various pa-
rameters (dropout, the size of the dense layers, ac-
tivation functions, CNN ﬁlter sizes and their num-
bers, pooling size, size of the GRU layer, and the op-
timization function) (see Appendix A for the search
space) using early stopping on the validation set. In
addition to these hyper-parameters, we also use the
validation set to pick the best number of segments
(N). Regarding the MultiSourceFake dataset, we
use 20% of the training part for validation. We rep-
resent words using pre-trained word2vec Google-
News-300 embeddings9. For evaluation, we follow
the setup from related work. We report accuracy
and weighted precision, recall and F1 score, and
macro F1 for some datasets where the classes are
imbalanced.
Baselines. To evaluate the performance of our
model, we use a combination of fake news detec-
tion models and deep neural network architectures:
• CNN, LSTM : We use CNN and LSTM mod-
els and validate their performance when treating
each document as one fragment. We experiment
with different hyper-parameters and report re-
sults for the ones that performed best on the
validation set.
• HAN: The authors of (Yang et al., 2016) pro-
posed a Hierarchical Attention Networks (HAN)
model for long document classiﬁcation. The pro-
posed model consists of two levels of attention
mechanisms, i.e., word and sentence attention.
The model splits each document into sentences
and learns sentence representations from words.
• BERT: is a text representation model that
showed superior performance on multiple natu-
ral language processing (NLP) benchmarks (De-
vlin et al., 2019). We use the pre-trained bert-
base-uncased version which has 12-layers and
yields output embeddings with a dimension of
size 768. We feed the hidden representation of
the special [CLS] token, that BERT uses to sum-
marize the full input sentence, to a softmax layer.
Experimentally, we found that ﬁne-tuning BERT
